sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source represents the northern segment of the Monti della Laga - Gorzano (MLG) fault system activated during the 2016-17 central Italy seismic sequence (e.g., Bonini et al., 2016; Valensise et al., 2016; Buttinelli et al., 2021).
This WSW-dipping normal fault system was formed during the Mesozoic and reactivated during the Miocene due to the flexure of the foreland in response of the orogenic building (Tondi et al., 2020). Later, during the development of the Acquasanta thrust sheet (Scisciani and Montefalcone, 2005), the MLG was transported onto the thrust hanging-wall.
The interpretation of seismic reflection profiles in the area (Porreca et al., 2018; Di Bucci et al., 2021, www.retrace3d.it) allowed to image a) the Acquasanta thrust geometry (Buttinelli et al., 2021), that dips toward W-NW, and b) the northern segment of MLG on its hanging-wall, that reaches seismogenic depths in the sector between the towns of Amatrice and Accumoli. To the north, while not mapped in the surface geology, MLG is overthrusted by the Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini (OAS) thrust near the Mt. Vettore. The sector of MLG north of Amatrice hosted the 24 August 2016 (Mw 6.0) mainshock (Bonini et al., 2016; Buttinelli et al., 2021). Conversely, the southern segment of the MLG near the Campotosto Lake is detached at a shallower level and the observed seismicity in this area (9 April 2009, Mw 5.4, and 18 January 2017, Mw 5.7) is located below the Acquasanta Thrust (Bigi et al., 2013; Buttinelli et al., 2021).
Historical and instrumental catalogues (ISIDe Working Group, 2007; Guidoboni et al., 2019; Rovida et al., 2021) show a very dense intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) to damaging seismicity within the area. The area covered by this Source has been affected by the 7 October 1639 (Mw 6.2) and the 28 April 1646 (Mw 5.9) Monti della Laga earthquakes (Galli et al., 2016).
This Source results from the extensive studies performed in the area following the 2016-17 seismic sequence (Michele et al., 2016; Chiaraluce et al., 2017; Improta et al., 2019; Michele et al., 2020) and the analysis of the 3D geological model built within the area (Di Bucci et al., 2021, www.retrace.it). Various investigators addressed the active tectonics and, subsequently, the seismogenic characteristics of the area, with widely divergent interpretations.
After the 24 August earthquake, ground ruptures were discontinuously identified along the MLG fault, whereas abundant ground ruptures were observed along the western flank of Mt. Vettore (EMERGEO Working Group, 2016, 2017; Civico et al., 2018; Villani et al., 2018). These were interpreted as primary coseismic ruptures (Pucci et al., 2017) or due to shaking-induced mechanisms, such as gravity-driven displacement, compaction, and secondary ground failure (Di Naccio et al., 2019).
The geodetic and seismological data highlight the presence of two main patches of slip during the 24 August 2016 earthquake (Tinti et al., 2016; Cheloni et al., 2017; Cirella et al., 2018), suggesting a complex rupture with a relatively high-angle dip in the southern sector (45Â°-50Â°) and a relatively low-angle dip in the northern sector (30Â°-40Â°), possibly involving the reactivation of inherited thrusts (Bonini et al., 2016) or a double fault system including the northern part of MLG fault and the Redentore-Vettoretto fault merging together at depth (Lavecchia et al., 2016).
Alternatively, Pizzi et al. (2017) propose that OAS splits the growing normal fault system (MLG to the south and Monte Vettore - Monte Bove to the north) and acted as a barrier for the 24 August 2016.
